name: keras
title: Keras: A Multi-Backend Deep Learning Framework for AI
answer: Keras is an open-source Python deep learning framework, now at version 3, that lets one codebase run on JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO. It sits at the model-building layer of the AI stack, offering layers, losses, optimizers, and training loops. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its multi-backend promise holds fully only for models built from built-in layers and keras.ops, so custom code may still tie you to a single backend.

sections.body: Keras is a Python deep learning framework maintained by the Keras team under the Apache-2.0 licence, with its source at github.com/keras-team/keras and documentation at keras.io. The site describes it simply as deep learning for humans. It occupies the model-building layer of the AI stack: you define layers, models, losses, optimizers, metrics, and training loops in Keras, while the numerical work runs on a chosen backend. Keras 3.0, the current major release announced on the official site, runs workflows on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO for inference only. The repository shows active development, with the last push recorded on 2 October 2026 and more than 64,000 stars.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Keras covers the concrete jobs of deep learning work: training, evaluation, and inference through fit, evaluate, and predict; data handling with NumPy arrays, tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects, and Pandas dataframes; and model construction through the Sequential API, the functional API, or subclassing. The official examples show image classification, autoencoders, transfer learning for small datasets, and a mini-GPT text generation model built with KerasHub. It is strongest when you want one readable codebase across backends, and the site notes that JAX typically delivers the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU, and CPU, though results vary by model and non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed for approachability, and the official guides walk a beginner from a first Sequential model through the functional API to custom losses and training loops. You need working Python and some familiarity with NumPy-style array thinking. The guides assume you understand concepts such as layers, activation functions, loss functions, optimizers, batch size, epochs, and validation splits, and they explain each in context rather than from first principles. Mathematics is not taught on the site, so a reader without basic linear algebra and calculus will need another source. The site offers complete runnable examples, including MNIST training that reaches roughly 95 percent test accuracy in two epochs, which makes the first successful run quick.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around Keras is broad. Keras 3 implements the full Keras API across TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch, including over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, training and evaluation loops, and saving and serialization infrastructure. The keras.ops namespace provides backend-agnostic operations such as matmul, sum, stack, einsum, softmax, binary crossentropy, and conv. KerasHub supplies pretrained models and layers, including the token and position embedding and Transformer decoder layers used in the mini-GPT example. The site states that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine. Documentation is extensive, with guides, examples, and API references on keras.io.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras serves both ends of the spectrum. For prototyping, the Sequential and functional APIs let you build and train a model in a few lines, and the built-in fit and evaluate loops handle batching, validation splits, and metric tracking without extra code. For production, the choice of backend matters: the site reports that JAX typically gives the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU, and CPU, while TensorFlow without XLA is occasionally faster on GPU. Keras 3 adds a distribution API in the keras.distribution namespace, currently implemented for the JAX backend with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon, which enables model parallelism, data parallelism, and combinations of both. The cost of the portable approach is that peak performance depends on backend selection and on staying within built-in layers and keras.ops.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The official site reports adoption by over 2.5 million developers and use in the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine, which places Keras among the current standards for applied deep learning rather than a legacy choice. Its multi-backend design means skills transfer across JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch workflows, and the site notes that existing tf.keras models using only built-in layers can run in JAX and PyTorch right away. For someone choosing what to learn, that breadth is useful, though the facts and the site do not give a breakdown of job listings or hiring demand, so claims about the job market beyond these named adopters would go beyond what the material supports.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is written in Python and is typically used alongside the frameworks it runs on: JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch, with OpenVINO supported for inference only. The polyglot pattern it belongs to is one where a high-level model definition language sits above interchangeable numerical engines. The site describes Keras as a low-level cross-framework language for developing custom components such as layers, models, or metrics that can then be used in native JAX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch workflows from one codebase. A Keras model can be instantiated as a PyTorch Module, exported as a TensorFlow SavedModel, or instantiated as a stateless JAX function, so it complements rather than replaces those frameworks.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The main limit stated on the official site is that portability across backends is guaranteed for models that use only built-in layers, and for custom code only as long as it relies on ops from keras.ops. The distribution API is implemented for the JAX backend, with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon, so parallelism features are uneven across backends. The site does not state which backend is best for every model, noting that benchmark results vary from model to model. It also does not give a detailed comparison against other high-level frameworks, a support policy, or guidance on migrating large existing codebases, so those questions remain open in the material reviewed.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
